title: Recording with Roy Brown for Deluxe
summary: First studio session; Roy Brown's absences and unpaid jobs; Fanny Brown and the 'don't tell nobody' background.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: But he wasn't a brainiest soloist. Mm-hm. Yeah. I wanted to talk to you about recordings you may have made. And do you remember the first time you went to a recording studio? Yeah.
And the first time I went to a recording studio, I recorded with Roy Brown. Okay.
Which, do you remember the?
Fanny Brown, if anybody had seen him as Fanny Brown. And where's my baseball bat? Mm-hm. And, oh, I forgot because it's been so long since I recorded it.
Were you in Roy Brown's band?
Yes and no. See, Roy, when he made this record, Lord of Miss, no, not Lord of Miss, Lord of Miss, when he did Fanny Brown, and I've heard the news. He was big.
Good Rockin' Night. Good Rockin' Night.
Yeah. Good Rockin' Night was his big hit. And then after that he recorded the thing, if anybody had seen Miss Fanny Brown, when I was on that record. And he, he, what do you want to say?
Were you just doing a pick-up date?

No. When he got popular, and he was so run behind women so much, he would have the band go play, and he wouldn't show up. And I played two jobs for him, and never got paid. Because the guy who gave the dance didn't want to pay him because he didn't play. The band played, but people came to hear Roy Brown.
So how did you get to get on the record? How did that work to record?
You know, well, he was, he wasn't popular at all before he made the record.
Right.

He made the record and everybody wanted to hire him. Sure. And women started running behind him, and he, he'd leave the job to be, to go to bed with a woman. And wouldn't show up for a couple of days. And the two jobs, I played with them twice, never did get paid. So the guy who gave the dance, he had the money, and he said, I said, well, mister, can you pay us? He said, no, who's in charge? I said, well, Roy. He said, I ain't pay nobody but Roy. So we didn't, he didn't pay us. So the union was supposed to get our money from Roy. But that was the funny thing. I think that the union and Roy made some kind of deal where Roy didn't have to pay, didn't have to pay us. And I think the union didn't put a fine on him. Because we never did hear anything. Every time we'd have a union meeting, we'd bring up about that money. They would close the meeting down. We'd say, well, look, we'll take that up next time, next month. We used to have a union meeting every month.
So you never ever saw the money from those jobs with Roy Brown. But you said you did a recording with Roy.
Yeah, well, we got paid for the recording. Because Roy, he didn't pay, he didn't have anything to do with the pay.
Now, who was recording for Deluxe, Deluxe Records? Yeah, Deluxe. And do you remember who was on that session? Who would have?

Clema Turbillon, Earl Barnes, Walter Daniel, Bob Ogden. I forgot who played bass. The music for the date? Yeah. Clema Turbillon. And most of the stuff was done at the studio. Roy didn't have enough songs to sing, so he was at the studio. Roy had to sing to remember to sing to remember to sing to remember to sing to remember to Roy didn't have enough songs to sing, so he was at that studio, and he would, he was in the back of the room, he was talking, he was writing out some lyrics, he said, well I got one now. So he asked Clement to put a background for the horns. So everything worked all right until we got to, has anybody here seen this Fanny Brown? Well Clement had run out of ideas, so he didn't know what to write in the background for him. So when Roy would say, has anybody here seen Miss Fanny Brown, and there was a big hole there, so Clement said, let's say, don't tell nobody. So he'd be putting, has anybody here seen Miss Fanny Brown, don't tell nobody has it, and he'd say, oh yeah, that's another thing that sold that record.
Oh yeah. Yeah, definitely. So you didn't have, did you have any input into the arrangement, or? I took a solo on this Mighty Mighty Man.

The first part, it started off with a trumpet solo. I've forgotten how it goes. Because Fanny Brown was the big side on it, on that record they had Fanny Brown on one side, Mighty Mighty Man on the other side. But Fanny Brown got more play.
Yeah.
Because of that thing. Don't tell nobody. Yeah.
